chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Abbas ibn Ma'ruf, from Safwan, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, from Minhal al-Qammad, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'Our companions seek to perform the 'Aqiqa when the Bedouins arrive, and they find the breeding males (of good quality), but when it is not that season, it is rare to find them for them.' He said: 'It is merely a sheep for meat; it is not in the same rank as the Udhiyah (sacrificial animal); anything goes from it.'

key_terms.الْأُضْحِيَّةُ: Al-Udhiyah: The sacrificial animal offered during Eid al-Adha
key_terms.الْإِبَّانُ: Al-iban: The proper season or time
key_terms.الْعَقِيقَةُ: Aqiqa: The sacrifice offered on the occasion of a child's birth
key_terms.الْفُحُولَ: Al-fuhul: Breeding males or prime animals of good quality
key_terms.يَجُوزُ مِنْهَا كُلُّ شَيْءٍ: Yajuzu minha kullu shay'in: All of it is permissible (to eat/use), indicating no specific parts are reserved or forbidden

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between Aqiqa and Udhiyah regarding the permissibility of eating the meat?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that the 'Aqiqa is fundamentally a sacrificial animal for consumption rather than a ritual with strict prohibitions, distinguishing it from the Udhiyah which carries specific legal restrictions. This ruling, transmitted through the chain of al-Qammāt, emphasizes the permissibility of utilizing all parts of the animal, reflecting the Shia juristic view that 'Aqiqa is a recommended act (mustahabb) focused on gratitude and feasting rather than a binding obligation with detailed constraints.
